sections.title: Conditional Probability
sections.content:
When the probability of an event A is calculated given that event B has already occurred, it is called Conditional Probability.
Formula: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)
Steps:
1. First find P(A ∩ B).
2. Then find P(B).
3. Divide the two.
Example: In a deck of 52 cards, if it is known that the card is Red, then the probability that it is a King = 2/26 = 1/13.

sections.title: Independent and Dependent Events
sections.content:
Independent: One event does not affect the other.
Formula: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B)
Dependent: One event affects the other.
Example (Independent): Tossing a coin and rolling a die together.
Example (Dependent): Drawing 2 cards without replacement.

sections.title: With Replacement vs Without Replacement
sections.content:
With Replacement: The total outcomes remain the same each time.
Example: From 5 red and 3 blue balls, getting red twice (with replacement)
P = (5/8) × (5/8)
Without Replacement: The total outcomes change each time.
P = (5/8) × (4/7)
This forms the basis of the Hypergeometric setup.

sections.title: Venn Diagram Based Problems
sections.content:
If out of 100 people, 60 read The Hindu, 50 read Times of India, and 20 read both:
1. Only Hindu = 60 − 20 = 40
2. Only TOI = 50 − 20 = 30
3. At least one = 60 + 50 − 20 = 90
Formula: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

sections.title: Basic Concept of Binomial Probability
sections.content:
When an event with probability p is repeated independently n times, the probability of exactly r successes is:
P = nCr × p^r × (1−p)^(n−r)
Example: Exactly 3 heads in 5 coins
= 5C3 × (1/2)^3 × (1/2)^2
= 10 × (1/32) = 10/32 = 5/16

sections.title: Use of Multiplication Theorem
sections.content:
Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)
Dependent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A)
It is important to determine whether events influence each other or not.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Confusing Independent and Dependent events.
2. Mistakes while calculating intersection.
3. Ignoring the replacement condition.
4. Forgetting nCr in Binomial probability.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content:
In conditional probability, always take the correct denominator.
Multiply probabilities for independent events.
Without replacement, the total decreases each time.
Remember the binomial formula: nCr × p^r × (1−p)^(n−r).

tricks.title: Quickly Identify Conditional Probability
tricks.explanation: If the question includes 'given that', it indicates conditional probability.

tricks.title: Identify Independent Events
tricks.explanation: If total outcomes do not change, treat them as independent.

tricks.title: Without Replacement Trick
tricks.explanation: Reduce the total by 1 each time.

tricks.title: Total Binomial Probability Equals 1
tricks.explanation: Adding probabilities for all r (from 0 to n) equals 1.
tricks.example: Sum of all outcomes in 5 trials → 1

tricks.title: Identify Exactly r Success
tricks.explanation: If the word 'exactly' appears, think of Binomial distribution.
